intro: What this build changed, in six places, each chosen by a rule from the build's own data. Tap one to go there.
method: Chosen by tools/ghent/showcase.mjs: one shot per criterion, never two of the same lot.

shots.title: A porch street: the 500 block of Mowbray Arch
shots.caption: 14 of 20 house fronts with a porch, on the even-numbered side.
why: Chosen as the block face in Ghent where the most house fronts get a porch: 14 of its 20 houses, among blocks with at least six.

Porches come from how often they appear in 121 of the City assessor's own street photos of Ghent: four in five houses have one, mostly on round columns behind white balusters, under a low hip roof (tools/ghent/yard-photos.md).

The City's footprints are traced from above, so a porch's roof is already inside them: here a porch is cut into the ground floor, a shaded recess with its columns at the wall, and only the steps, the walk and the yard come out in front.
shots.look_for: Round columns and balusters, the shade of the porch, steps down to clipped boxwoods along the foundation.

shots.title: 1615 Colonial Avenue: a coffee shop on a porch
shots.caption: The house keeps its porch, door and windows; a coffee shop shows through them.
why: Chosen as the converted café or bistro whose house keeps the widest porch (15.8 m): adaptive reuse in one frame.
Its ground floor would hold a coffee shop (a small restaurant or café), up to 2,754 sq ft. Why it may: On an arterial or collector street, in a Sustain place type.
Doors and windows stay where they are: the building is adapted, not remodelled. The new use shows through its own windows, with a sign over the door.
shots.look_for: The sign over the door, the lit windows, the porch as it was.

shots.title: 703 W Princess Anne Road: porches stacked
shots.caption: An apartment building's porch, one storey on another.
why: Chosen as the apartment building with the widest stacked porch (19.8 m across, 4 storeys).
In the assessor's photos, half the apartment buildings' porches are stacked two or more storeys (13 of 26), several three or four tiers; their railings are mostly iron, their roofs mostly flat.
shots.look_for: The second porch over the first, its railing, the columns running up through both.

shots.title: Two-tone houses: the 600 block of Westover Avenue
shots.caption: 6 of 11 houses brick below, shingle or siding above.
why: Chosen as the block face with the most two-tone houses: 6 of 11.

A third of the houses in the assessor's photos are two-tone, mostly a brick ground floor with shingle or siding above, so walls are painted by building type from those photos: brick for most apartment buildings, and for houses brick, two-tone, siding, shingle or stucco in the photos' proportions.
shots.look_for: The line where the brick stops and the shingle begins, a storey up.

shots.title: Lanterns
shots.caption: 16 Colonial lanterns within 45 m of each other.
why: Chosen as the densest run of Colonial lanterns: 16 within 45 m of each other, where Dominion Energy's records (the City's open data) put them.

670 of the 1160 streetlights in and by the League's area are Colonials, by our reading of the data's fixture codes against Dominion's catalogue: a lantern on a 13-foot pole. The rest are cobra heads and shoeboxes on arms over the busier streets, and floodlights.
shots.look_for: The lanterns lit along the sidewalk, and their pools of light.

shots.title: 737 Graydon Avenue: a hardware store, five minutes from 247 lots
shots.caption: It would bring hardware within five minutes of 247 lots where today it's more than ten.
why: Chosen as the ground floor that would change the most neighbours' weeks, among the weekly needs (coffee, bread, groceries, hardware, a haircut, dry cleaning): if it opened, 247 lots would have a place for hardware within a five-minute walk where today the nearest is more than ten minutes away.
Walks run along the City's street centerlines at 3 miles an hour (ours); today's places are Overture Maps' (open, at confidence 0.6 or more). Day to day shows it from any lot.

The map opens every ground floor the proposal would allow; Policy Brief No. 2 expects far fewer: “a steady state of 15–40 in years 6–10”. At that pace, any one of them has about a 8% to 21% chance of opening.
shots.look_for: Its sign and its lit windows; then open Day to day from here.
